rv.q: Bartlett Sher’s production, featuring legions of kids and lashings of costumes, purrs like a Rolls-Royce.
As drama, on the other hand, the saccharine piece lumbers along.
It’s a vibrant moment in Sher’s staid production, which takes the heavy-handed dialogue at a ponderous pace.
Yes, it’s a flawed, at times cursory-feeling piece, but it has a gentleness and innocent charm that’s as much a saving grace as a sign of its post-war origins.
The King and I is undoubtedly dated, but it still retains its charm.
Rodgers & Hammerstein’s musical is still magnificent in its way, but this starchy production does little to address its problems...
Bartlett Sher’s revival of his 2015 US production comes to London after a year-long UK tour: it’s technically competent but stolid and stale.
Golden Age musical pleasures with a dash of contemporary wisdom: it’s a pretty heady combination.
When it’s presented as entertainingly as it is here, it’s hard to resist.

It may not be a dynamic night in the theatre, but it remains a constantly engaging one, watchable at worst and entrancing at best, unfolding at a leisurely pace, that could be construed as soporific if you were feeling uncharitable.

The costumes cannot make up for the teasing set design that promises much with the opening scene—an impressive boat on which Anna arrives in Siam—but then disappointingly delivers nothing else remotely in the same league.
But as good as the songs are, you can’t get away from the fact this is a bit of a clunky, old-fashioned musical with themes that may have been acceptable in 1951 but are a little dated now.
This King and I is a rapturous, immensely likeable production that doesn't push the envelope for the simple reason that no one saw the need.

cn.t: Bartlett Sher's lavish production pleases crowds with gorgeous songs and spectacle, but critics note the musical's dated, problematic white-savior narrative feels increasingly uncomfortable in 2024, despite Helen George's poised performance.
